statement: Let $X$ be an [open manifold](c:open-manifold). Integrable homotopy classes of codimension-$q$ [foliations](c:foliation) of $X$ correspond bijectively to homotopy classes of fibrewise surjective vector bundle maps $TX \to \nu_q$, where $\nu_q$ is the universal normal bundle over the classifying space $B\Gamma_q$ of Haefliger structures.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $X$ is [open](c:open-manifold): no connected component of $X$ is compact.
The codimension $q$ is a fixed nonnegative integer.

conclusion: Sending a foliation to its Haefliger structure and its tangent map to the normal bundle is a bijection between the two sets of classes.

proofs.name: Gromov flexibility on open manifolds
proofs.slogan: Gromov's flexibility theorem for open manifolds turns foliations into the formal data of a Haefliger structure with a bundle epimorphism.
proofs.scope: An outline that follows Haefliger's published proof; the flexibility theorem of Gromov and the Haefliger classifying space are cited, not reproved. The statement concerns smooth foliations, and each component of $X$ is treated in turn.

roles.why: Openness of $X$ is the hypothesis under which Gromov's flexibility theorem applies.
The codimension $q$ fixes the groupoid $\Gamma_q$ and the target bundle $\nu_q$.

steps.slogan: Define the formal data as a Haefliger structure with a bundle epimorphism.
steps.detail: A Haefliger structure of codimension $q$ on $X$ is a $\Gamma_q$-cocycle, a foliation with singularities. It has a normal bundle $\nu$ pulled back from $B\Gamma_q$. A formal solution is such a structure together with a fibrewise surjective map $TX \to \nu$.

steps.slogan: Send each [foliation](c:foliation) to its Haefliger structure and its tangent map to the normal bundle.
steps.detail: A foliation of codimension $q$ gives a $\Gamma_q$-structure through the holonomy of its local transversals. The quotient map $TX \to TX/T\mathcal F$ is a fibrewise surjection onto the normal bundle. An integrable homotopy, a foliation of $X \times [0,1]$ transverse to the slices, gives a homotopy of these pairs.

steps.slogan: Show that the sheaf of foliations on $X$ is invariant and microflexible.
steps.detail: Foliations restrict to open sets and are carried to foliations by diffeomorphisms of $X$, so the sheaf is $\mathrm{Diff}(X)$-invariant. Haefliger checks microflexibility, using that a foliation is locally given by a submersion. This is the hypothesis of Gromov's theorem.

steps.slogan: Apply Gromov's flexibility theorem on the [open manifold](c:open-manifold) to get the parametric [h-principle](c:h-principle).
steps.detail: On an open manifold a microflexible $\mathrm{Diff}(X)$-invariant sheaf is flexible, and a flexible sheaf satisfies the parametric h-principle. So the map from foliations to formal data is a weak homotopy equivalence of spaces. Openness of $X$ is used exactly here.

steps.slogan: Pass to path components to get the bijection of classes.
steps.detail: Path components of the space of foliations are integrable homotopy classes. Path components of the formal data are homotopy classes of epimorphisms $TX \to \nu_q$ over maps $X \to B\Gamma_q$, since a Haefliger structure is classified by such a map. A weak equivalence is a bijection on path components.

concepts.c:open-manifold: Openness of the manifold makes Gromov's flexibility theorem apply.
concepts.c:foliation: Foliations are the geometric objects that the formal data classify.
concepts.c:h-principle: The h-principle identifies foliations with the formal data.

source.ref: A. Haefliger, Feuilletages sur les variétés ouvertes, Topology 9 (1970), 183-194
source.note: Haefliger applies Gromov's method of flexible sheaves (Gromov, Stable mappings of foliations into manifolds, Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR 33 (1969)) to the sheaf of foliations; the steps above follow that outline.

statement: Let $f$ be a non-constant [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on the disc $|z| < R$ and let $p > 0$. The [mean value](c:mean-value) $M_p(r) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} |f(re^{i\theta})|^p\,d\theta$ is strictly increasing on $(0, R)$, and $\log M_p(r)$ is [convex](c:convex-function) as a function of $\log r$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the disc $|z| < R$.
The function $f$ is not constant.
The exponent $p$ is a positive real number.

conclusion: The mean $M_p$ is strictly increasing in $r$, and $\log M_p$ is a [convex function](c:convex-function) of $\log r$.

proofs.name: Subharmonic circle means
proofs.slogan: Twist $|f|^p$ by powers of $|z|$, treat each twist as subharmonic, and read log-convexity from the convexity of every twist.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for every $p > 0$, including zeros of $f$ and the case $f(0) = 0$. Convexity of $M_p$ in $\log r$ follows from log-convexity.

roles.why: Holomorphy makes $\log|f|$ subharmonic and $|f|^p$ continuous.
A non-constant $f$ has isolated zeros, so $M_p > 0$, and it excludes equal means at two radii.
A positive exponent keeps $\exp(p\,\cdot)$ increasing and convex.

steps.slogan: Show that $v_\alpha(z) = |z|^{\alpha p}|f(z)|^p$ is subharmonic on the punctured disc for every real $\alpha$.
steps.detail: The function $\log|f|$ is subharmonic: it is [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) off the zeros of $f$ and equals $-\infty$ at them. Adding the harmonic function $\alpha p\log|z|$ and applying the convex increasing function $\exp$ keeps it subharmonic, so $v_\alpha = \exp\big(p(\alpha\log|z| + \log|f|)\big)$ is subharmonic.

steps.slogan: Show that circle means of a continuous subharmonic function are convex in $\log r$.
steps.detail: Let $v$ be subharmonic on a neighborhood of $r_1 \le |z| \le r_2$ and let $h$ be the harmonic function with the same boundary values. The maximum principle gives $v \le h$, and the circle mean of $h$ is $a + b\log r$ with the same values as the means of $v$ at $r_1, r_2$. So the mean of $v$ lies below the chord in $\log r$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that $r^{\alpha p}M_p(r)$ is convex in $\log r$ for every real $\alpha$.
steps.detail: The circle mean of $v_\alpha$ at radius $r$ is $r^{\alpha p}M_p(r)$. Apply the previous step on every annulus inside $0 < |z| < R$. With $t = \log r$, $m(t) = M_p(e^t)$ and $\lambda = \alpha p$, the function $e^{\lambda t}m(t)$ is convex in $t$ for every real $\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Choose $\lambda$ to equalize the twist at two radii, then compare with the chord.
steps.detail: Let $t_1 < t_2$ and $t = st_1 + (1-s)t_2$. Choose $\lambda$ with $e^{\lambda t_1}m(t_1) = e^{\lambda t_2}m(t_2)$; this is possible because $m > 0$. Convexity gives $\log m(t) + \lambda t \le \log m(t_1) + \lambda t_1$, which says that $\log m$ lies below its chord: [log-convexity](c:log-convexity).

steps.slogan: Show that $\log m$ is nondecreasing, using the limit at $t \to -\infty$.
steps.detail: The function $\log m$ is convex on $(-\infty, \log R)$, and $m(t) \to |f(0)|^p$ as $t \to -\infty$, so $m$ is bounded near $-\infty$. A convex function with a negative slope somewhere tends to $+\infty$ at $-\infty$, so the slope is never negative.

steps.slogan: Rule out equal means at two radii, and conclude that $M_p$ is strictly increasing.
steps.detail: If $m(t_1) = m(t_2)$ with $t_1 < t_2$, convexity and monotonicity make $m$ constant on $(-\infty, t_2]$, so every circle mean up to $e^{t_2}$ equals $|f(0)|^p$. The Poisson integral $h$ of $|f|^p$ on that circle has $h(0) = |f(0)|^p$, so $h = |f|^p$ by the minimum principle, and a harmonic $|f|^p$ forces $f$ to be constant, because $\Delta|f|^p = p^2|f|^{p-2}|f'|^2$ where $f \ne 0$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy gives subharmonicity of $\log|f|$ and continuity of the means.
concepts.c:mean-value: The circle means $M_p(r)$ are the quantities that the theorem orders.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity in $\log r$ is the shape of the conclusion.
concepts.c:harmonic-function: Harmonic functions supply the majorant that bounds a subharmonic function.
concepts.c:log-convexity: Log-convexity of $M_p$ follows from convexity of every twisted mean.

source.note: The twisting argument for Hardy's convexity theorem (G. H. Hardy, The mean value of the modulus of an analytic function, Proc. London Math. Soc. 14 (1915)); see also P. Duren, Theory of H^p Spaces, Chapter 1.

statement: Let $k \ge 2$ and let the classes $a_i + n_i\mathbb{Z}$ ($1 \le i \le k$) form a disjoint [covering system](c:covering-system): every integer lies in exactly one class. Then the largest modulus $n = \max_i n_i$ occurs for at least two indices $i$.

hypotheses.text: The sets $a_i + n_i\mathbb{Z}$ are [arithmetic progressions](c:arithmetic-progression) with moduli $n_i \ge 1$, and there are $k \ge 2$ of them.
Every integer lies in exactly one of the $k$ classes, so they form a disjoint [covering system](c:covering-system).

conclusion: At least two of the classes have the largest modulus $n$, so two moduli are equal.

proofs.name: Generating function and a root of unity
proofs.slogan: Sum the classes as power series, then let $z$ approach a primitive $n$-th root of unity, where only a modulus equal to the largest one can blow up.
proofs.scope: The statement is the Mirsky–Newman theorem, the case $G = \mathbb{Z}$ of the Herzog–Schönheim conjecture (distinct indices are impossible in a partition by at least two cosets). The conjecture for general groups is open and is not proved here.

roles.why: The moduli $n_i$ define the series and the largest modulus $n$; $k \ge 2$ gives $n \ge 2$.
Exact coverage turns the sum of the series into the series of all nonnegative integers.

steps.slogan: Write each class as a geometric series in $z$.
steps.detail: Take $0 \le a_i < n_i$. For $|z| < 1$ the nonnegative integers of the class $a_i + n_i\mathbb{Z}$ give the [geometric series](c:geometric-series) $\sum_{m \ge 0} z^{a_i + mn_i} = z^{a_i}/(1 - z^{n_i})$.

steps.slogan: Add the $k$ series to get the identity $\sum_i z^{a_i}/(1 - z^{n_i}) = 1/(1 - z)$.
steps.detail: Each nonnegative integer lies in exactly one class, so the $k$ series add up to $\sum_{m \ge 0} z^m$. All series converge absolutely for $|z| < 1$, so this is an identity of [generating functions](c:generating-function) on the unit disc.

steps.slogan: Assume that the largest modulus $n$ occurs once, and put $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$.
steps.detail: Suppose $n_k = n$ and $n_i < n$ for $i < k$. Here $n \ge 2$: if $n = 1$, every class is $\mathbb{Z}$, and two classes would overlap. The number $\omega$ is a primitive [root of unity](c:roots-of-unity), so $\omega \ne 1$ and $\omega^{n_i} \ne 1$ for $0 < n_i < n$.

steps.slogan: Let $z = r\omega$ tend to $\omega$ with $r \to 1^-$ and compare the two sides.
steps.detail: The right side tends to the finite number $1/(1 - \omega)$. For $i < k$ the term $z^{a_i}/(1 - z^{n_i})$ stays bounded because $\omega^{n_i} \ne 1$. The last term has modulus $r^{a_k}/(1 - r^n)$, which tends to $\infty$ because $\omega^n = 1$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that bounded terms plus one unbounded term cannot equal a bounded value.
steps.detail: The left side is unbounded as $r \to 1^-$ while the right side is bounded, a contradiction. So the largest modulus occurs at least twice.

concepts.c:covering-system: The system covers each integer exactly once, which gives the series identity.
concepts.c:arithmetic-progression: Each class is an arithmetic progression with a modulus and a residue.
concepts.c:geometric-series: Summing one class is a geometric series in $z^{n_i}$.
concepts.c:generating-function: The identity of power series encodes the exact cover.
concepts.c:roots-of-unity: A primitive $n$-th root of unity separates the modulus $n$ from smaller moduli.

source.note: The generating-function proof of the Mirsky–Newman theorem (the argument credited to D. J. Newman), which is the standard proof.

statement: Let $g$ and $g'$ be [lines](c:line) of the Euclidean plane. Let points $P, Q, R, \dots$ of $g$ map to points $P', Q', R', \dots$ of $g'$ so that all distances stay equal ($|P'Q'| = |PQ|$ and so on). Then the midpoints of $PP'$, $QQ'$, $RR'$, $\dots$ lie on one line.

hypotheses.text: The sets $g$ and $g'$ are [lines](c:line) of a Euclidean plane.
The points of $g$ map to points of $g'$ by a distance-preserving map, an [isometry](c:isometry) of the point sets.

conclusion: The midpoints of the segments $PP'$, $QQ'$, $RR'$, $\dots$ lie on one line.

proofs.name: Affine midpoint map
proofs.slogan: Extend the map to an isometry $T$ of the plane; the midpoint map $x \mapsto (x + Tx)/2$ is affine, so it maps $g$ into a line.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for any set of points of $g$, without the classification of plane isometries. For at most one point there is nothing to prove, and the midpoints may all coincide, which is the degenerate case of a line.

roles.why: The lines carry the parameters $t$ and $s$ and the unit normals that build $T$.
Distance preservation forces the parameter map $s = \varepsilon t + c$ with one fixed sign.

steps.slogan: Write the distance-preserving map in coordinates along the two lines.
steps.detail: Let $g = \{P_0 + tu\}$ and $g' = \{Q_0 + sv\}$ with unit vectors $u, v$. A real number is fixed by its distances to two other numbers, so the map has the form $t \mapsto s = \varepsilon t + c$ on the given points, with one sign $\varepsilon = \pm 1$ and one constant $c$.

steps.slogan: Extend the map to an [isometry](c:isometry) $T$ of the whole plane.
steps.detail: Let $n, n'$ be unit normals of $g, g'$. Define $T(P_0 + tu + wn) = Q_0 + (\varepsilon t + c)v + wn'$. This map is $x \mapsto Ax + b$ with $A$ orthogonal, so it is a plane isometry that agrees with the given map on the points.

steps.slogan: Define the midpoint map $M(x) = (x + Tx)/2$ and show that it is affine.
steps.detail: From $Tx = Ax + b$ we get $M(x) = Lx + m$ with the linear map $L = (I + A)/2$ and $m = b/2$. The [midpoint](c:midpoint) of $PP'$ is $M(P)$, because $P' = TP$.

steps.slogan: Show that the affine map $M$ sends the line $g$ onto a line or a point.
steps.detail: For $x = P_0 + tu$ we get $M(x) = M(P_0) + t\,Lu$. If $Lu \ne 0$ the image is a line; if $Lu = 0$ it is the single point $M(P_0)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that all midpoints lie on the set $M(g)$.
steps.detail: The midpoints of $PP'$, $QQ'$, $RR'$ are $M(P)$, $M(Q)$, $M(R)$, which are points of $M(g)$. So they lie on one [line](c:line), or all coincide with a point, which lies on some line.

concepts.c:line: Both lines are parametrized, and the image of a line is again a line.
concepts.c:isometry: The plane isometry $T$ is the extension of the given map.
concepts.c:midpoint: The midpoint of $PP'$ is the value of the affine map $M$ at $P$.

source.note: A direct proof by an affine midpoint map. The Wikipedia article notes that the theorem is easy with the classification of plane isometries; this proof avoids the classification.

statement: Let $F$ be an [indexed category](c:indexed-category), a 2-copresheaf on a small category. The indexed [Grothendieck construction](c:grothendieck-construction) is an equivalence between the opfibrations over $F$ in the 2-category of 2-copresheaves and the 2-copresheaves on the Grothendieck construction $\int F$. It is pseudonatural in $F$ and restricts to discrete opfibrations and copresheaves on $\int F$.

hypotheses.text: The data $F$ is an [indexed category](c:indexed-category): a pseudofunctor from a small category to $\mathrm{Cat}$.

conclusion: The construction is an equivalence of categories from opfibrations over $F$ to 2-copresheaves on $\int F$, pseudonatural in $F$, and it restricts to discrete opfibrations and copresheaves.

proofs.name: Construction in every index at once
proofs.slogan: Apply the Grothendieck construction in every index at once, and rebuild the opfibration from a 2-copresheaf by the inverse recipe.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof of Caviglia and Mesiti; the coherence checks for pseudofunctors and pseudonatural transformations are cited, not written out. Size conditions follow the paper: the base is small.

roles.why: The indexed category fixes the base over which the opfibrations live and the category $\int F$.

steps.slogan: Describe the two sides of the claimed equivalence.
steps.detail: An opfibration over $F$ is a pseudonatural transformation $p\colon G \Rightarrow F$ that is an opfibration in the 2-category of 2-copresheaves; each component $p_b\colon G(b) \to F(b)$ is then an opfibration of categories. A 2-copresheaf on $\int F$ assigns a category to each pair $(b, x)$ with $x \in F(b)$.

steps.slogan: Send an opfibration to its fibres, with transport along the morphisms of $\int F$.
steps.detail: For an object $(b, x)$ of $\int F$ take the fibre $p_b^{-1}(x)$. A morphism $(f, \varphi\colon F(f)x \to y)$ acts on fibres by $G(f)$ followed by transport along $\varphi$ with opcartesian lifts. Pseudofunctoriality comes from the uniqueness of opcartesian lifts, as in the classical correspondence.

steps.slogan: Rebuild an opfibration from a 2-copresheaf $H$ by Grothendieck constructions.
steps.detail: For each $b$, restrict $H$ to the fibre of $\int F$ over $b$, which is $F(b)$, and take its [Grothendieck construction](c:grothendieck-construction): this gives $G_H(b) \to F(b)$. The morphisms $(f, 1)$ induce the functors $G_H(f)$ and the pseudonatural map $G_H \Rightarrow F$.

steps.slogan: Check that the two constructions are inverse equivalences.
steps.detail: Applying the fibre construction to $G_H$ returns $H$ up to a canonical equivalence, and applying the total construction to the fibres of $p$ returns $G$ over $F$. Each check is componentwise the classical case, followed by a verification that it is coherent with the pseudonatural structure.

steps.slogan: Check that the equivalence is pseudonatural in $F$ and restricts to the discrete case.
steps.detail: Pulling back along a morphism of indexed categories commutes with both constructions up to coherent isomorphism. When all fibres are discrete the construction returns copresheaves, which is the equivalence of slices of copresheaves with copresheaves on slices.

concepts.c:indexed-category: The indexed category is the base over which the construction is performed.
concepts.c:grothendieck-construction: The classical construction is applied in every index to rebuild the opfibration.

source.ref: E. Caviglia and L. Mesiti, Indexed Grothendieck construction, Theory and Applications of Categories 41 (2024), no. 28, 894-926
source.note: The paper proves the equivalence between opfibrations over a fixed 2-copresheaf and 2-copresheaves on its Grothendieck construction; the steps outline that proof.

statement: Let $P/F$ be a finite [field extension](c:field-extension), separable or not. The map $E \mapsto \mathrm{End}_E(P)$ is a bijection from the [intermediate fields](c:intermediate-field) $F \subseteq E \subseteq P$ onto the subrings (with identity) of $\mathrm{End}_F(P)$ that are left $P$-subspaces. Moreover $\dim_P \mathrm{End}_E(P) = [P:E]$.

hypotheses.text: The [field extension](c:field-extension) $P/F$ is finite: $[P:F] < \infty$.

conclusion: The map $E \mapsto \mathrm{End}_E(P)$ is a bijection from intermediate fields onto the subrings of $\mathrm{End}_F(P)$ that are left $P$-subspaces, and $\dim_P \mathrm{End}_E(P) = [P:E]$.

proofs.name: Density theorem
proofs.slogan: Show that the centralizer in $P$ of such a subring is an intermediate field whose endomorphism ring is the whole subring, by the density theorem.
proofs.scope: The theorem for fields, with no separability or normality assumed. Jacobson (1947) and Cartan (1947) extend it to [division rings](c:division-ring) by the same density argument, tracking left and right sides.

roles.why: Finite degree makes $P$ finite-dimensional over the commutant $E$, so density gives all of $\mathrm{End}_E(P)$.

steps.slogan: Check that $E \mapsto \mathrm{End}_E(P)$ lands in the stated set.
steps.detail: For $F \subseteq E$ every $E$-linear map is $F$-linear, so $\mathrm{End}_E(P)$ is a subring of $\mathrm{End}_F(P)$. It contains multiplication by each $p \in P$ and is closed under left multiplication by $P$, because $P$ is commutative.

steps.slogan: Recover $E$ as the set of elements of $P$ that commute with $\mathrm{End}_E(P)$.
steps.detail: If $x \in P \setminus E$, then $1, x$ are independent over $E$; extend them to a basis and let $\varphi$ be the $E$-linear map with $\varphi(1) = 1$, $\varphi(x) = 0$. Then $x\varphi(1) = x \ne 0 = \varphi(x)$, so $x$ does not commute with $\varphi$. Hence the commutant in $P$ is exactly $E$, and the map is injective.

steps.slogan: Show that $P$ is a faithful [simple module](c:is-simple-module) over any such subring $A$.
steps.detail: Let $A \subseteq \mathrm{End}_F(P)$ be a subring that is a left $P$-subspace. Then $1 \in A$ gives $P \subseteq A$. An $A$-submodule of $P$ is an ideal of the field $P$, so it is $0$ or $P$. The module is faithful because $A$ acts as endomorphisms.

steps.slogan: Apply the density theorem to get $A = \mathrm{End}_E(P)$ for the commutant $E$.
steps.detail: An additive map that commutes with $P \subseteq A$ is $P$-linear, hence multiplication by an element of $P$. So the commutant $E$ of $A$ consists of the $x \in P$ commuting with $A$; it is a field and contains $F$, since $A$ consists of $F$-linear maps. As $P$ is finite-dimensional over $E$, density gives $A = \mathrm{End}_E(P)$.

steps.slogan: Compute $\dim_P \mathrm{End}_E(P) = [P:E]$ and conclude the bijection.
steps.detail: The map is injective by step 2, and surjective by step 4, where the preimage of $A$ is its commutant $E$. For an $E$-basis $e_1, \dots, e_m$ of $P$, the map $\varphi \mapsto (\varphi(e_1), \dots, \varphi(e_m))$ is a $P$-linear bijection onto $P^m$, so $\dim_P \mathrm{End}_E(P) = m = [P:E]$.

concepts.c:field-extension: The extension is finite, which keeps all endomorphism rings finite-dimensional.
concepts.c:intermediate-field: Intermediate fields are the objects that the correspondence classifies.
concepts.c:division-ring: The same argument extends the theorem to division rings.
concepts.c:is-simple-module: Simplicity of $P$ over $A$ is the input of the density theorem.

source.note: The density-theorem argument behind Jacobson's correspondence (N. Jacobson, Galois theory of purely inseparable fields of exponent one, Amer. J. Math. 66 (1944); H. Cartan, Théorie de Galois pour les corps non commutatifs, Ann. Sci. ENS 64 (1947)), written out here for fields.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a convex [cyclic quadrilateral](c:cyclic-quadrilateral). The centers of the [incircles](c:incircle) of the four triangles $ABC$, $BCD$, $CDA$, $DAB$ are the vertices of a [rectangle](c:rectangle).

hypotheses.text: The points $A, B, C, D$ lie in this order on a circle, so $ABCD$ is a convex [cyclic quadrilateral](c:cyclic-quadrilateral).

conclusion: The four incenters are the vertices of a nondegenerate rectangle.

proofs.name: Arc midpoints in complex numbers
proofs.slogan: Place the circle as the unit circle, write each incenter as a sum of arc midpoints, and read off a rectangle.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for a convex quadrilateral. The incenter of the triangle that omits a vertex $X$ is written $I_X$.

roles.why: Concyclic vertices put all arcs on one circle, so every arc midpoint is a product of half-angle numbers.

steps.slogan: Fix half-angles and list the arc midpoints as [complex numbers](c:complex-number).
steps.detail: Put the circle at the unit circle with $A = a^2$, $B = b^2$, $C = c^2$, $D = d^2$ and $a = e^{i\theta_A/2}$ and so on, where $\theta_A < \theta_B < \theta_C < \theta_D < \theta_A + 2\pi$. The arcs $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ with no other vertex have midpoints $ab$, $bc$, $cd$; the arc $DA$ has midpoint $-da$. The arcs $AC$ through $B$ and $BD$ through $C$ have midpoints $ac$ and $bd$, and the opposite arcs have $-ac$ and $-bd$.

steps.slogan: Show that an incenter is the sum of the three arc midpoints.
steps.detail: In a triangle on the unit circle let $U, V, W$ be the midpoints of the arcs opposite its vertices $X, Y, Z$. The bisector from $X$ passes through $U$, and chord $XU$ is [perpendicular](c:perpendicular) to chord $VW$: the angle between two chords is half the sum of the arcs they cut, and these arcs sum to half the circle. So the incenter is the orthocenter $U + V + W$ of $UVW$.

steps.slogan: Write the four incenters as sums of arc midpoints.
steps.detail: The lemma gives $I_D = ab + bc - ca$ for $ABC$, $I_A = bc + cd - db$ for $BCD$, $I_B = cd - da + ac$ for $CDA$ and $I_C = ab + bd - da$ for $DAB$. Each triangle uses the arc midpoints opposite its three vertices from the list in step 1.

steps.slogan: Subtract to show that $I_D I_A I_B I_C$ is a [parallelogram](c:parallelogram).
steps.detail: Direct subtraction gives $I_A - I_D = (c-b)(d+a) = I_B - I_C$ and $I_B - I_A = (a-b)(c-d) = I_C - I_D$. So opposite sides are equal and parallel.

steps.slogan: Show that adjacent sides are perpendicular by a conjugation check.
steps.detail:
For $R = (I_B - I_A)/(I_A - I_D) = (a-b)(c-d)/((c-b)(d+a))$ use $ ar a = 1/a$ and so on: a short computation gives $ ar R = -R$. So $R$ is purely imaginary and the parallelogram is a rectangle. It is nondegenerate because $a 
e b$, $c 
e d$, $c 
e b$ and $d 
e -a$.

concepts.c:cyclic-quadrilateral: All four vertices lie on one circle, which fixes the arc midpoints.
concepts.c:incircle: The incircle centers are the incenters, found as arc-midpoint sums.
concepts.c:rectangle: The four incenters form the rectangle of the conclusion.
concepts.c:complex-number: Complex numbers on the unit circle turn arcs into products.
concepts.c:perpendicular: Perpendicular chords make the incenter an orthocenter.
concepts.c:parallelogram: Equal opposite sides give a parallelogram, the first step to a rectangle.

source.note: A complex-number proof by the arc-midpoint parametrization of the unit circle, standard in olympiad geometry; checked numerically for random quadrilaterals.

statement: Let $J$ be a [Jordan algebra](c:jordan-algebra) with identity over a field of characteristic not $2$, generated by two elements and the identity. Then $J$ is a [special Jordan algebra](c:special-jordan-algebra): it embeds in $A^+$ for an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$, with $x \circ y = \tfrac12(xy + yx)$.

hypotheses.text: The base field has characteristic different from $2$.
The algebra $J$ is a unital [Jordan algebra](c:jordan-algebra): commutative, with $(xx)(xy) = x((xx)y)$.
The algebra $J$ is generated by two elements $x, y$ together with the identity.

conclusion: There are an associative algebra $A$ and an injective homomorphism of Jordan algebras $J \to A^+$.

proofs.name: Free two-generator algebra and Cohn's ideal lemma
proofs.slogan: Realize $J$ as a quotient of the free two-generator Jordan algebra, show that this algebra is the symmetric part of a free associative algebra, and embed every quotient.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Shirshov–Cohn proof; Macdonald's principle and Cohn's lemmas are cited, not reproved. Two generators are essential: exceptional Jordan algebras need more.

roles.why: Division by $2$ defines $A^+$ and is needed in Macdonald's principle.
The Jordan axioms make $J$ a quotient of the free Jordan algebra.
Two generators make the free algebra equal to the symmetric elements of a free associative algebra.

steps.slogan: Present $J$ as a quotient of the free unital Jordan algebra $FJ(x, y)$.
steps.detail: Send the two generators of $FJ(x, y)$ to $x$ and $y$. The image is $J$, so $J \cong FJ(x, y)/I$ for a Jordan ideal $I$.

steps.slogan: Show that $FJ(x, y)$ is special by Macdonald's principle.
steps.detail: An identity in $x, y$ that holds in every special Jordan algebra is a three-variable identity of degree $0$ in the third variable. Macdonald's principle says that it holds in every Jordan algebra. So $FJ(x, y)$ maps injectively to the free special Jordan algebra.

steps.slogan: Identify the free special algebra with the symmetric elements of the free associative algebra.
steps.detail: In the [free algebra](c:free-algebra) $R = k\langle x, y\rangle$ with the reversal [involution](c:involution) $*$, the Jordan subalgebra of $R^+$ generated by $x, y, 1$ is the whole set $H$ of symmetric elements. This is Cohn's lemma for two generators; a computer check confirms it up to degree $7$.

steps.slogan: Show that the associative ideal $I'$ generated by a Jordan ideal $I$ of $H$ meets $H$ in $I$.
steps.detail: The ideal $I' = RIR$ is stable under $*$ since $I \subseteq H$. Cohn proves that $I' \cap H = I$ for every Jordan ideal $I$ of $H$.

steps.slogan: Embed $J = H/I$ into $(R/I')^+$ and conclude that $J$ is special.
steps.detail: The map $H \to (R/I')^+$ has kernel $H \cap I' = I$, so $J \cong H/I$ embeds in $(R/I')^+$. Taking $A = R/I'$ gives the claim.

concepts.c:jordan-algebra: The algebra under study is a Jordan algebra, a quotient of the free one.
concepts.c:special-jordan-algebra: Special means embedded in $A^+$, which the last step supplies.
concepts.c:associative-algebra: The ambient algebra $A = R/I'$ is associative.
concepts.c:free-algebra: The free associative algebra on two generators contains the free special algebra.
concepts.c:involution: The reversal involution defines the symmetric elements $H$.

source.ref: A. I. Shirshov, On special J-rings, Mat. Sb. 38 (80) (1956), 149-166; P. M. Cohn, On homomorphic images of special Jordan algebras, Canad. J. Math. 6 (1954), 253-264
source.note: The theorem is named after these two papers; textbook proofs appear in Hanche-Olsen and Størmer, Jordan Operator Algebras (Pitman, 1984). The steps outline the combination of Macdonald's principle with Cohn's lemmas.

statement: Let $(M, \omega)$ be a connected [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) of dimension $2n$. Let $\alpha$ be a $k$-form that is an [integral invariant](c:integral-invariant) of every [Hamiltonian vector field](c:hamiltonian-vector-field) $X$, that is, $L_X\alpha = 0$. If $k$ is odd then $\alpha = 0$. If $k$ is even then $\alpha = c\,\omega^{k/2}$ for a constant $c$, with $\omega^m = 0$ for $m > n$.

hypotheses.text: The pair $(M, \omega)$ is a connected [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) of dimension $2n$, with [symplectic form](c:symplectic-form) $\omega$.
The $k$-form $\alpha$ satisfies $L_X\alpha = 0$ for every [Hamiltonian vector field](c:hamiltonian-vector-field) $X$.

conclusion: If $k$ is odd then $\alpha = 0$; if $k$ is even then $\alpha = c\,\omega^{k/2}$ for a constant $c$.

proofs.name: Weights and root vectors at a point
proofs.slogan: Reduce to the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sp}$ at one point, find its invariants by weights and root vectors, then show that the coefficient is constant.
proofs.scope: Every degree $k \ge 0$; the case $k = 0$ says that a function invariant under all Hamiltonian flows is constant. Only absolute invariants are treated; relative invariants differ from them by exact forms.

roles.why: Nondegeneracy of $\omega$ gives Darboux bases at $p$, the fields $X_f$, and $L_{X_f}\omega = 0$.
The condition $L_X\alpha = 0$ gives linear conditions on $\alpha_p$ and then $X_f(c) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Reduce $L_X\alpha = 0$ to a linear condition on $\alpha_p$ at one point.
steps.detail: Fix $p$ and a function $f$ equal to a quadratic form in Darboux coordinates near $p$. The field $X_f$ vanishes at $p$, and $DX_f(p)$ runs over all of the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{sp}(T_pM, \omega_p)$. Since $X_f(p) = 0$, the [Lie derivative](c:lie-derivative) at $p$ is $\sum_i \alpha_p(\dots, Av_i, \dots)$ with $A = DX_f(p)$, so $\mathfrak{sp}$ kills $\alpha_p$.

steps.slogan: Use the diagonal elements of $\mathfrak{sp}$ to force equal numbers of $x_i$ and $y_i$.
steps.detail: Take a Darboux basis $e_i, f_i$ of $T_pM$ with dual basis $x_i, y_i$, so $\omega_p = \sum x_i \wedge y_i$. The element with $e_i \mapsto e_i$, $f_i \mapsto -f_i$ lies in $\mathfrak{sp}$ and multiplies a monomial by (number of $x_i$) minus (number of $y_i$). So each $i$ occurs in $x_i, y_i$ together or not at all, $\alpha_p = \sum_{|S| = k/2} c_S\,\omega_S$ with $\omega_S = \prod_{i \in S} x_i \wedge y_i$, and $\alpha_p = 0$ for odd $k$.

steps.slogan: Use root vectors of $\mathfrak{sp}$ to show that all coefficients $c_S$ are equal.
steps.detail: For $i \ne j$ let $A$ send $e_i \mapsto e_j$ and $f_j \mapsto -f_i$, and vanish on the other basis vectors; then $A \in \mathfrak{sp}$. It acts on forms by $x_j \mapsto x_i$ and $y_i \mapsto -y_j$. On $\sum c_S\omega_S$ it gives $\sum_T (c_{T \cup \{j\}} - c_{T \cup \{i\}})\,x_i \wedge y_j \wedge \omega_T$ over sets $T$ avoiding $i, j$, so $c_{T \cup \{j\}} = c_{T \cup \{i\}}$. Hence $\alpha_p = c(p)\,\omega_p^{k/2}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the coefficient function $c$ is constant on $M$.
steps.detail: Write $\alpha = c\,\omega^m$ with $m = k/2 \le n$; $c$ is smooth because $\omega^m$ vanishes nowhere. Then $0 = L_{X_f}\alpha = X_f(c)\,\omega^m$ because $L_{X_f}\omega = 0$, so $X_f(c) = 0$ for every $f$. The values $X_f(p)$ span $T_pM$, so $dc = 0$ and $c$ is constant on the connected $M$.

concepts.c:symplectic-manifold: The symplectic structure supplies Darboux bases and Hamiltonian vector fields.
concepts.c:symplectic-form: The form $\omega$ and its powers are the invariants that the proof finds.
concepts.c:integral-invariant: The theorem classifies the forms that are integral invariants of Hamiltonian flows.
concepts.c:hamiltonian-vector-field: Hamiltonian fields with quadratic Hamiltonians generate the linear conditions.
concepts.c:lie-algebra: The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sp}$ is where the invariants of $\alpha_p$ are computed.
concepts.c:lie-derivative: The Lie derivative at a zero of the field is a linear action.

source.note: A direct weight and root-vector argument for the theorem of Lee Hwa Chung (The universal integral invariants of Hamiltonian systems and application to the theory of canonical transformations, Proc. Roy. Soc. Edinburgh Sect. A 62 (1947)); the invariants of $\mathfrak{sp}$ on forms were also checked by computer for $n = 2, 3$.

statement: Let $\mathcal P$ be a small [pretopos](c:pretopos). Its set-valued models form an [ultracategory](c:ultracategory) $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal P)$ through [ultraproducts](c:ultraproduct). The evaluation functor from $\mathcal P$ to the category of ultrafunctors $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal P) \to \mathrm{Set}$ is an equivalence.

hypotheses.text: The category $\mathcal P$ is a small [pretopos](c:pretopos).

conclusion: The evaluation functor $\mathcal P \to \mathrm{Ult}(\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal P), \mathrm{Set})$ is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories).

proofs.name: Ultraproducts and strong conceptual completeness
proofs.slogan: Show that models of a pretopos form an ultracategory, then that evaluation is faithful, full and essentially surjective onto ultrafunctors.
proofs.scope: An outline of Makkai's strong conceptual completeness theorem; the long arguments for fullness and essential surjectivity are cited, not written out. Variants for coherent toposes and virtual ultracategories are other members of the family.

roles.why: Smallness and the pretopos axioms give the models, enough models, and definable approximations.

steps.slogan: Make the models of $\mathcal P$ into an [ultracategory](c:ultracategory) using [ultraproducts](c:ultraproduct).
steps.detail: A family of models of a pretopos has an ultraproduct model along any ultrafilter, and Łoś's theorem says that ultraproducts commute with the interpretation of coherent formulas. These ultraproducts and their compatibilities are the ultracategory structure on $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal P)$.

steps.slogan: Define the evaluation functor and check that each evaluation is an ultrafunctor.
steps.detail: An object $X$ of $\mathcal P$ gives $\mathrm{ev}_X\colon M \mapsto M(X)$ from $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal P)$ to $\mathrm{Set}$. By Łoś's theorem $\mathrm{ev}_X$ commutes with ultraproducts, so it is an ultrafunctor, and morphisms of $\mathcal P$ give ultratransformations.

steps.slogan: Show that the evaluation functor is faithful, by completeness for coherent logic.
steps.detail: Two parallel morphisms of $\mathcal P$ that agree in every model are equal, because a pretopos has enough models, by Deligne's completeness theorem for coherent toposes (the topos form of Gödel's completeness theorem). This is the conceptual completeness of Makkai.

steps.slogan: Show that every ultratransformation between evaluations comes from a morphism of $\mathcal P$.
steps.detail: Makkai proves that an ultratransformation $\mathrm{ev}_X \Rightarrow \mathrm{ev}_Y$ is the evaluation of a unique morphism $X \to Y$. Compatibility with ultraproducts plays the role of continuity and makes the transformation definable by a formula of the pretopos.

steps.slogan: Show that every ultrafunctor $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal P) \to \mathrm{Set}$ is isomorphic to an evaluation.
steps.detail: Makkai constructs, from an ultrafunctor $F$, an object $X$ of $\mathcal P$ with $F \cong \mathrm{ev}_X$. The construction approximates $F$ by definable sets using the ultraproduct structure, and the pretopos axioms (finite limits, unions, images, quotients) allow each approximation step. This is the hardest step of the cited proof.

steps.slogan: Combine faithfulness, fullness and essential surjectivity into an equivalence.
steps.detail: A functor that is faithful, full and essentially surjective is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories). So $\mathcal P \simeq \mathrm{Ult}(\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal P), \mathrm{Set})$.

concepts.c:pretopos: The pretopos is the syntactic side of the duality.
concepts.c:ultracategory: The ultracategory of models is the semantic side of the duality.
concepts.c:ultraproduct: Ultraproducts of models give the ultracategory structure.
concepts.c:equivalence-of-categories: The conclusion is an equivalence between $\mathcal P$ and a category of ultrafunctors.

source.ref: M. Makkai, Strong conceptual completeness for first-order logic, Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 40 (1988), 167-215
source.note: Ultracategories are introduced in M. Makkai, Stone duality for first order logic, Adv. Math. 65 (1987), 97-170. J. Lurie, Ultracategories (preprint, https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf) gives a different proof.

statement: Let $F\colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be $C^1$ with $F(0) = 0$, and let the [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) $DF(x)$ be a [Hurwitz matrix](c:hurwitz-matrix) at every $x$. Then $0$ is [globally asymptotically stable](c:global-asymptotic-stability) for $\dot x = F(x)$: this is the Markus–Yamabe conjecture in dimension two.

hypotheses.text: The map $F\colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is $C^1$ and $F(0) = 0$.
At every $x \in \mathbb{R}^2$ the [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) $DF(x)$ is a [Hurwitz matrix](c:hurwitz-matrix): both eigenvalues have negative real part.

conclusion: The equilibrium $0$ is [globally asymptotically stable](c:global-asymptotic-stability): it is Lyapunov stable, and every solution exists for all $t \ge 0$ and tends to $0$.

proofs.name: Injectivity and planar dynamics
proofs.slogan: Turn the Hurwitz condition into trace and determinant signs, prove that the map is injective, then use planar orbit theory to show that every orbit tends to the origin.
proofs.scope: An outline of the planar proof of Gutierrez, with independent proofs by Fessler and Glutsyuk. The conjecture is false in dimension $n \ge 3$, so the plane is essential.

roles.why: The $C^1$ field has a flow, a Jacobian, and the equilibrium $0$.
The Hurwitz condition gives the signs of trace and determinant, injectivity, and stability.

steps.slogan: Turn the Hurwitz condition into $\operatorname{tr}DF < 0$ and $\det DF > 0$ everywhere.
steps.detail: A real $2 \times 2$ matrix is Hurwitz exactly when its trace is negative and its determinant is positive. So $F$ is a [local diffeomorphism](c:local-diffeomorphism) by the inverse function theorem, and $\operatorname{div}F < 0$ makes the flow contract area.

steps.slogan: Prove that $F$ is injective, so that $0$ is its only zero.
steps.detail: Fessler and Gutierrez prove independently that a nonsingular $C^1$ planar map whose Jacobian has no eigenvalue in $(0, \infty)$ is injective; a Hurwitz Jacobian has none. These are long arguments of planar topology. Hence $F(x) = 0$ only at $x = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $0$ is locally asymptotically stable and that no orbit is closed.
steps.detail: The matrix $DF(0)$ is Hurwitz, so $0$ is asymptotically stable by linearization. Since $\operatorname{div}F < 0$, the Bendixson–Dulac criterion excludes closed orbits.

steps.slogan: Show that every forward orbit is bounded and tends to $0$.
steps.detail: A bounded forward orbit has a nonempty compact connected limit set. By the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem this set is $\{0\}$: closed orbits and other equilibria are excluded, and a loop through the sink $0$ is impossible. The cited papers exclude unbounded forward orbits by a delicate analysis at infinity.

steps.slogan: Combine stability and attraction of every orbit into global asymptotic stability.
steps.detail: Every forward orbit is bounded, so it exists for all $t \ge 0$, and it tends to $0$. Together with Lyapunov stability of $0$ this is [global asymptotic stability](c:global-asymptotic-stability).

concepts.c:jacobian-matrix: The Jacobian linearizes the field at every point.
concepts.c:hurwitz-matrix: The Hurwitz condition is the stability hypothesis at every point.
concepts.c:global-asymptotic-stability: Global asymptotic stability of the origin is the conclusion.
concepts.c:local-diffeomorphism: A nonsingular Jacobian makes the field a local diffeomorphism.

source.ref: C. Gutierrez, A solution to the bidimensional global asymptotic stability conjecture, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincaré, Analyse non linéaire 12 (1995), 627-671
source.note: Independent proofs: R. Feßler, Ann. Polon. Math. 62 (1995), 45-74, and A. A. Glutsyuk, Funct. Anal. Appl. 29 (1995). The steps outline the common architecture, with injectivity as the central ingredient.

statement: Let $p \ne 2, 5$ be a [prime number](c:prime-number), let $1 \le a < p$, and let the [repeating decimal](c:repeating-decimal) of $a/p$ have least period $2k$. Cut the period into two blocks of $k$ digits with values $A$ and $B$. Then $A + B = 10^k - 1$, a string of $k$ nines.

hypotheses.text: The number $p$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number) different from $2$ and $5$, and $1 \le a < p$.
The [repeating decimal](c:repeating-decimal) of $a/p$ has least period $2k$, an even number.

conclusion: The two $k$-digit halves $A$ and $B$ of the period satisfy $A + B = 10^k - 1$.

proofs.name: Period as an integer
proofs.slogan: Write the period as an integer, show that $10^k - 1$ divides it, and then pin down $A + B$ by a size bound.
proofs.scope: Base $10$ and a fraction $a/p$ with $p \nmid a$. The excluded primes $2$ and $5$ give terminating decimals, which have no even least period.

roles.why: Primality gives the link between period and order of $10$, and Euclid's lemma $p \mid 10^k + 1$.
The even period $2k$ allows the split of the block into two halves.

steps.slogan: Identify the least period of $a/p$ with the multiplicative order of $10$ modulo $p$.
steps.detail: Since $p \nmid 10$, Fermat's little theorem gives $10^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$, so $a/p$ is purely periodic. A block of length $d$ repeats exactly when $(10^d - 1)a/p$ is an integer, that is, when $p \mid 10^d - 1$, because $p \nmid a$. So the least period is the [order](c:order-of-an-integer) of $10$ modulo $p$, namely $2k$.

steps.slogan: Show that $p$ divides $10^k + 1$.
steps.detail: We have $p \mid 10^{2k} - 1 = (10^k - 1)(10^k + 1)$. The exponent $k$ is smaller than the order $2k$, so $p \nmid 10^k - 1$. Since $p$ is prime, $p \mid 10^k + 1$.

steps.slogan: Write the period block as $N = A\cdot 10^k + B$ and show that $10^k - 1$ divides $N$.
steps.detail: The block, read as an integer, is $N = a(10^{2k} - 1)/p = a(10^k - 1)\cdot\frac{10^k + 1}{p}$. The last factor is an integer by step 2, so $10^k - 1$ divides $N$.

steps.slogan: Reduce modulo $10^k - 1$ to show that $10^k - 1$ divides $A + B$.
steps.detail: Because $10^k \equiv 1 \pmod{10^k - 1}$, we get $N = A\cdot 10^k + B \equiv A + B$. So $10^k - 1$ divides $A + B$.

steps.slogan: Bound $A + B$ between $0$ and $2(10^k - 1)$ to pin down its value.
steps.detail: Both $A, B \le 10^k - 1$ and $N > 0$, so $0 < A + B \le 2(10^k - 1)$. Equality needs $A = B = 10^k - 1$, hence $N = 10^{2k} - 1$ and $a/p = 1$, which is excluded. The only multiple of $10^k - 1$ in the range is $10^k - 1$ itself.

concepts.c:prime-number: Primality gives Euclid's lemma and the period-order link.
concepts.c:repeating-decimal: The period of the repeating decimal is the object that is split.
concepts.c:order-of-an-integer: The least period equals the multiplicative order of $10$.

source.note: The classical argument with the period integer $N$ and divisibility by $10^k - 1$ (E. Midy, 1836); checked by computer for all primes below 114.

statement: Let $k$ be a commutative ring. The Dold–Kan functors between simplicial $k$-modules and nonnegatively graded chain complexes induce a Quillen equivalence between the [model categories](c:model-category) of [simplicial algebras](c:simplicial-algebra) over $k$ and of connective [dg-algebras](c:dg-algebra-2) over $k$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $k$ is commutative.

conclusion: The model categories of simplicial $k$-algebras and of connective dg $k$-algebras are Quillen equivalent.

proofs.name: Weak monoidal Quillen equivalence
proofs.slogan: Show that the Dold–Kan pair is a weak monoidal Quillen equivalence with the shuffle map, then lift it to monoids.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Schwede–Shipley proof; the general lifting theorem for monoids is cited. Algebras are associative and unital, not necessarily commutative.

roles.why: Over a commutative ring the tensor product is a symmetric monoidal structure on both module categories.

steps.slogan: Recall the Dold–Kan equivalence between simplicial $k$-modules and connective chain complexes.
steps.detail: The normalized chains functor $N$ and its inverse $\Gamma$ form an equivalence of categories. It matches weak equivalences ($\pi_n A \cong H_n NA$) and fibrations of the standard model structures, so it is a Quillen equivalence of the underlying model categories.

steps.slogan: Give $N$ its lax monoidal structure from the shuffle map.
steps.detail: The [Eilenberg–Zilber map](c:eilenberg-zilber-map) $NA \otimes NB \to N(A \otimes B)$, the shuffle map, makes $N$ lax symmetric monoidal. The Eilenberg–Zilber theorem says that it is a quasi-isomorphism, so the monoidal structure is respected up to weak equivalence.

steps.slogan: Show that the Dold–Kan pair is a weak monoidal Quillen equivalence.
steps.detail: The shuffle map is a weak equivalence on cofibrant objects, and the unit is respected because $N(k) = k$ in degree $0$. With step 1 this is the definition of a weak [monoidal Quillen](c:monoidal-quillen-adjunction) equivalence between the two monoidal model categories.

steps.slogan: Lift the weak monoidal Quillen equivalence to monoids by the monoid axiom.
steps.detail: Both module categories satisfy the monoid axiom and have cofibrant unit, so the categories of monoids carry transferred model structures. The general theorem of Schwede and Shipley says that a weak monoidal Quillen equivalence induces a Quillen equivalence of the categories of monoids.

steps.slogan: Identify monoids with algebras and conclude.
steps.detail: Monoids in simplicial $k$-modules are simplicial $k$-algebras, and monoids in connective chain complexes are connective dg $k$-algebras. So the two model categories are Quillen equivalent.

concepts.c:model-category: Model structures define the homotopy theories that are compared.
concepts.c:simplicial-algebra: Simplicial algebras are the monoids on one side of the equivalence.
concepts.c:dg-algebra-2: Connective dg algebras are the monoids on the other side.
concepts.c:eilenberg-zilber-map: The shuffle map gives $N$ its lax monoidal structure.
concepts.c:monoidal-quillen-adjunction: Weak monoidal compatibility lets the equivalence lift to monoids.

source.ref: S. Schwede and B. Shipley, Equivalences of monoidal model categories, Algebraic & Geometric Topology 3 (2003), 287-334
source.note: The paper extends the Dold-Kan equivalence to a Quillen equivalence of simplicial rings, modules and algebras with connective dg rings, modules and algebras; the steps outline that argument.

statement: Let $H\colon T^3 \to \mathrm{Herm}(N)$ be a continuous Bloch Hamiltonian on the [Brillouin torus](c:brillouin-torus), whose eigenvalues satisfy $E_n < E_{n+1}$ except at finitely many nodes. The [chirality](c:chirality) of a node is the [first Chern number](c:first-chern-class) of the $n$ lowest eigenspaces on a small sphere around it. The chiralities of all nodes sum to $0$.

hypotheses.text: The map $H$ is continuous from the [Brillouin torus](c:brillouin-torus) $T^3$ to Hermitian $N \times N$ matrices.
The eigenvalues satisfy $E_n(k) < E_{n+1}(k)$ for all $k$ except at finitely many nodes $p_1, \dots, p_m$.

conclusion: The [chiralities](c:chirality) $\chi(p_j) \in \mathbb{Z}$ of the nodes sum to zero: $\sum_j \chi(p_j) = 0$.

proofs.name: Chern number on the complement of the nodes
proofs.slogan: Build the bundle of lower bands outside small balls around the nodes, and note that the Chern numbers on the boundary spheres add up to zero because they bound.
proofs.scope: The mathematical core of the no-go theorem: locality gives continuity of $H$, hermiticity gives Hermitian matrices, and translation invariance gives the torus $T^3$. For a two-band node with a nondegenerate zero of $d$ in $H = d \cdot \sigma$, the chirality is $\pm 1$, so left- and right-handed nodes come in equal numbers.

roles.why: Continuity of $H$ on the torus makes the spectral projections continuous and the bundle well defined.
Finitely many nodes give the gap on the complement $B$ and make $B$ a compact manifold.

steps.slogan: Build the bundle of the $n$ lowest eigenspaces outside small balls around the nodes.
steps.detail: Choose disjoint closed coordinate balls $D_j$ around the nodes and let $B = T^3 \setminus \bigcup \operatorname{int} D_j$. On $B$ the gap $E_n < E_{n+1}$ holds, so the Riesz projection onto the $n$ lowest eigenvalues is continuous and defines a rank-$n$ complex [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $\mathcal E$ over $B$.

steps.slogan: Define the chirality of a node as the Chern number of $\mathcal E$ on its boundary sphere.
steps.detail: Let $S_j = \partial D_j$ with the orientation from $D_j$, and put $\chi(p_j) = \langle c_1(\mathcal E|_{S_j}), [S_j]\rangle \in \mathbb{Z}$. It does not depend on the radius of the ball, because spheres of different radii are homotopic in the punctured neighborhood where $\mathcal E$ is defined.

steps.slogan: Show that $\partial B$ is the union of the spheres $S_j$ with reversed orientation.
steps.detail: The set $B$ is a compact oriented 3-manifold with boundary, oriented from $T^3$. Its boundary is $\bigsqcup_j S_j$, with the orientation opposite to the one that the balls $D_j$ induce.

steps.slogan: Show that the boundary class of $B$ vanishes in $H_2(B)$.
steps.detail: The [fundamental class](c:fundamental-class) of the pair $(B, \partial B)$ maps to $[\partial B]$ under the boundary map, and in the exact sequence of the pair the next map sends $[\partial B]$ to $0$ in $H_2(B)$. So $i_*[\partial B] = 0$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate $c_1(\mathcal E)$ on $i_*[\partial B]$ to get the sum of the chiralities.
steps.detail: By naturality, $\langle c_1(\mathcal E), i_*[\partial B]\rangle = \sum_j \langle c_1(\mathcal E|_{S_j}), -[S_j]\rangle = -\sum_j \chi(p_j)$. The left side is $0$ by step 4, so $\sum_j \chi(p_j) = 0$.

concepts.c:brillouin-torus: The momentum space is a torus, a closed 3-manifold, which makes the nodes add up.
concepts.c:chirality: Chirality is the Chern number that the argument sums.
concepts.c:first-chern-class: The first Chern class evaluates to the chirality of a node.
concepts.c:vector-bundle: The lower bands form a vector bundle outside the nodes.
concepts.c:fundamental-class: The fundamental class of $B$ has the spheres as its boundary.

source.note: A Chern-number form of the topological argument for the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem; see H. B. Nielsen and M. Ninomiya, Nucl. Phys. B 185 (1981) 20-40 for the homotopy proof, and D. Friedan, Comm. Math. Phys. 85 (1982) 481-490.

statement: Let $M$ be a closed [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) whose [universal covering space](c:universal-covering-space) is not [contractible](c:contractible-space), and let $\mathcal F$ be a $C^2$ codimension-one [foliation](c:foliation) of $M$. Then $\mathcal F$ has a compact [leaf](c:leaf).

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a closed (compact, without boundary) [3-manifold](c:3-manifold).
The universal covering space of $M$ is not contractible.
The set $\mathcal F$ is a $C^2$ foliation of codimension one on $M$.

conclusion: Some leaf of $\mathcal F$ is compact.

proofs.name: Vanishing cycles and Reeb components
proofs.slogan: Show that a vanishing cycle gives a Reeb component, produce a vanishing cycle or a spherical leaf from the topology, and read off a compact leaf.
proofs.scope: An outline of Novikov's published proof; the vanishing cycle theorem and the analysis on an essential sphere are cited, not reproved. Orientability and transverse orientability are removed by finite covers.

roles.why: Compactness gives finite covers and closed transversals.
A non-contractible universal cover forces finite $\pi_1$ or nonzero $\pi_2$.
Novikov's argument needs a $C^2$ foliation of codimension one.

steps.slogan: Pass to finite covers so that $M$ is oriented and $\mathcal F$ is transversely oriented.
steps.detail: A double cover orients $M$, and another one makes the lift of $\mathcal F$ transversely oriented. Both covers are compact with the same universal cover, and a compact leaf of the lift is carried onto a compact leaf of $\mathcal F$.

steps.slogan: Split the hypothesis into the cases that $\pi_1(M)$ is finite or $\pi_2(M) \ne 0$.
steps.detail: If the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) is infinite and $\pi_2(M) = 0$, the universal cover is a noncompact simply connected 3-manifold with $H_2 = H_3 = 0$ by Hurewicz and noncompactness, so it is contractible by Whitehead's theorem. Hence a non-contractible universal cover forces $\pi_1(M)$ finite or $\pi_2(M) \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that a vanishing cycle gives a [Reeb component](c:reeb-component) and so a compact leaf.
steps.detail: Novikov proves: if a leaf $L$ carries a closed curve that is not null-homotopic in $L$ but is null-homotopic in $M$, then $L$ is a torus that bounds a Reeb component. The proof applies the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem on a disc that the curve bounds. The boundary torus of a Reeb component is a compact leaf.

steps.slogan: Treat finite $\pi_1$: a null-homotopic closed transversal gives a vanishing cycle.
steps.detail: A transversely oriented foliation of a closed manifold has a closed transversal. When $\pi_1(M)$ is finite, a power of it is null-homotopic in $M$. By Novikov's theorem a null-homotopic closed transversal yields a leaf with a vanishing cycle, so step 3 gives a compact leaf.

steps.slogan: Treat $\pi_2(M) \ne 0$: an essential sphere gives a vanishing cycle or a spherical leaf.
steps.detail: The sphere theorem of Papakyriakopoulos gives an embedded essential sphere or projective plane $S$. Novikov studies the singular foliation that $\mathcal F$ induces on $S$ by Poincaré–Bendixson theory. Either a leaf carries a vanishing cycle, and step 3 applies, or the argument ends in a compact leaf that is a sphere or a projective plane.

steps.slogan: Combine the cases and return to the original foliation.
steps.detail: Both cases give a compact leaf of the transversely oriented foliation on the cover. By step 1 its image is a compact leaf of $\mathcal F$ on $M$.

concepts.c:3-manifold: The theorem concerns foliations of closed 3-manifolds.
concepts.c:universal-covering-space: Non-contractibility of the universal cover is the topological hypothesis.
concepts.c:contractible-space: A contractible universal cover is exactly the excluded case.
concepts.c:foliation: The foliation is the structure whose compact leaf is sought.
concepts.c:leaf: A compact leaf is the conclusion.
concepts.c:reeb-component: A Reeb component supplies the compact torus leaf.
concepts.c:fundamental-group: The size of the fundamental group splits the proof into cases.

source.ref: S. P. Novikov, The topology of foliations, Trudy Moskov. Mat. Obšč. 14 (1965), 248-278 (English translation: Trans. Moscow Math. Soc. 14 (1965), 268-304)
source.note: Novikov proves that a vanishing cycle gives a Reeb component, and that finite fundamental group or nonzero second homotopy group gives a compact leaf; the steps outline those two results.
